summary: Describes how to carry G.722.1 audio bitstreams in RTP packets, including the details needed for MIME and SDP. It is on the standards track. It was replaced by RFC 5577.

eli5.summary: To send voice over the Internet in small packages, the sender and receiver need to agree on how to pack it. This explains it for one voice format. A newer document later replaced it.

questions: how to send g.722.1 audio over rtp
subtitle: How to send G.722.1 wideband audio over RTP

tldr.problem: G.722.1 is a wideband audio codec, but applications need a standard way to carry it in RTP packets along with details for MIME and SDP signaling.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3047 specifies the RTP payload format for G.722.1, including how to pack encoded frames into RTP packets, the MIME type audio/G7221, and SDP parameters including the required bitrate field.
tldr.outcome: Applications can now reliably send and receive G.722.1 audio over RTP in real-time communications, streaming, and messaging. RFC 5577 later provided an updated specification.

today: RFC 3047 was replaced by RFC 5577, which provides an updated RTP payload format specification for G.722.1.

sections.title: Overview of G.722.1
sections.content: G.722.1 is an ITU-T standard audio codec that compresses audio from 50 Hz to 7 kHz into one of two standard bitrates: 24 kbit/s or 32 kbit/s. It is a low-complexity coder suitable for real-time communication like videoconferencing and telephony, as well as streaming audio and messaging applications. The codec operates with a fixed frame size of 20 milliseconds, and the number of bits per frame is constant for a given bitrate.
sections.eli5: G.722.1 is a codec that squeezes voice to one of two speeds: 24,000 bits per second or 32,000 bits per second, using 20-millisecond chunks.

sections.title: RTP Payload Format
sections.content:
G.722.1 uses a 16 kHz sampling rate clock, so RTP timestamps are in units of 1/16000 of a second. The payload contains one or more frames of G.722.1 data directly, with no additional header specific to this payload format. At 24 kbit/s, each 20 ms frame produces 480 bits (60 octets); at 32 kbit/s, it produces 640 bits (80 octets). Both align on octet boundaries without needing padding.

The encoding algorithm uses variable-length coding (like Huffman coding) within the fixed frame, making it impossible to identify individual encoded parameters without decoding the entire frame. For RTP packetization, this does not matter: the payload format simply preserves the bit sequence from the encoder. Multiple frames can be packed into a single RTP packet, provided they all have the same bitrate, and frames must not be split across packet boundaries.
sections.eli5: The data goes directly into RTP packets: 60 bytes for 24 kbit/s, or 80 bytes for 32 kbit/s, for each 20 ms chunk. You can fit many chunks in one packet.

sections.title: MIME and SDP Parameters
sections.content:
The MIME type is audio/G7221. The bitrate parameter is required because the bitrate is not signaled in the G.722.1 bitstream itself. Standard bitrates are 24000 and 32000; non-standard bitrates are allowed (from 16000 to 32000, as multiples of 400) to maintain octet alignment. The optional ptime parameter specifies the recommended duration in milliseconds of each RTP packet.

In SDP, the encoding name is G7221 (same as the MIME subtype). An SDP example: m=audio 49000 RTP/AVP 121 with a=rtpmap:121 G7221/16000 and a=fmtp:121 bitrate=24000.
sections.eli5: The official name is audio/G7221. You must tell the other side which bitrate (24000 or 32000) you are using, because it is not included in the audio data itself.

sections.title: Security and DoS Considerations
sections.content: RTP packets using this payload format are subject to the security considerations in the RTP specification and applicable RTP profiles. Confidentiality of media streams is achieved by encryption applied after compression, with no conflict between the two. G.722.1 compression does not exhibit significant non-uniform receiver computational load, so there is no particular denial-of-service risk from complex frames. As with any IP-based protocol, a receiver may be overloaded by receiving too many packets; network-layer authentication and multicast pruning can help mitigate this.
sections.eli5: Use encryption to protect the audio if needed. The codec does not have any weird tricks that would let someone attack it with crafted packets.
